tasks.title: Famous astronomical events
tasks.statement:
Arrange the following astronomy-related events in chronological order from the oldest to the most recent. Write the correct serial number (between 1 and 11) in the appropriate box on the answer sheet.
       1. Launch of the Hubble Space Telescope
       2. Viking probes arrived at planet Mars
       3. Discovery of Phobos and Deimos
       4. Latest perihelion of comet 1/P Halley
       5. Discovery of Ceres (asteroid / dwarf planet)
       6. Discovery of Uranus (planet)
       7. First successful measurement of a stellar parallax
       8. Discovery of the first planetary nebula
       9. Discovery of stellar populations (I and II)
       10. First identification of a quasar with an optical source
       11. Discovery of the expansion of the Universe

parts.question: Arrange the 11 events in chronological order.
parts.reference:
Correct solution:
  1. 1764: Discovery of the first planetary nebula
  2. 1781: Discovery of Uranus
  3. 1801: Discovery of Ceres
  4. 1838: First successful measurement of a stellar parallax
  5. 1877: Discovery of Phobos and Deimos
  6. 1929: Discovery of the expansion of the Universe
  7. 1943: Discovery of stellar populations
  8. 1963: First identification of a quasar with an optical source
  9. 1976: Viking probes arrived at planet Mars
 10. 1986: Latest perihelion of comet 1/P Halley
 11. 1990: Launch of the Hubble Space Telescope
The score of the faultless order is 10 points. The list will be checked pairwise. In each case when a later event precedes an earlier event in your solution, one point will be deducted.

tasks.title: Deflection of radio photons in the gravitational field of solar system bodies
tasks.statement:
A. Eddington and F. Dyson from Principe, and C. Davidson and A. Crommelin from Sobral, Brazil measured the deflection of light coming from stars apparently very close to the Sun during the total solar eclipse in 1919. The deflection was found to agree with the theoretically predicted value of 1.75''. A light ray (or photon) which passes the Sun at a distance $d$ is deflected by an angle
$$\Delta\theta \propto \frac{4GM_\odot}{dc^2}$$
The present-day accuracy of the VLBI (Very Long Baseline Interferometry) technique in the radio wavelength range is 0.1 mas (milliarcsecond). Is it possible to detect a deflection of radio photons from a quasar by (a) Jupiter, (b) the Moon? Estimate the angle of deflection in both cases and mark "YES" or "NO" on the answer sheet.

parts.question: Is it possible to detect a deflection of radio photons from a quasar by Jupiter? Estimate the angle of deflection and mark "YES" or "NO".
parts.reference:
One has to notice that in the case of the Sun d = R, that is d equals the solar radius. The angular deflection scales as m/r (mass over radius) of the deflector body, so one has to consider Mb /Rb , where b stands for Jupiter and Moon, respectively.
$$\frac{\Delta\theta_b}{\Delta\theta} = \frac{M_b /R_b}{M/R}$$
$$\Delta\theta_b = \Delta\theta \frac{M_b /R_b}{M/R}$$
a) Jupiter
Substituting the masses and radii one gets:
$\Delta\theta_J = 0.017^{\circ\prime} = 17 \text{ mas}$
The deflection of radio waves by Jupiter’s gravitational field is greater than 0.1 mas, so it is observable with the VLBI network. The answer is: YES

parts.question: Is it possible to detect a deflection of radio photons from a quasar by the Moon? Estimate the angle of deflection and mark "YES" or "NO".
parts.reference:
b) Moon
Substituting the masses and radii one gets:
$\Delta\theta_M = 0.000026^{\circ\prime} = 0.026 \text{ mas}$
The deflection of radio waves by Moon’s gravitational field is smaller than 0.1 mas, so it is not observable with the VLBI network. The answer is: NO

tasks.title: The supermassive black hole in the centre of Milky Way Galaxy and M87
tasks.statement: The first image of a black hole was constructed recently by the international team of the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT). The imaged area surrounds the supermassive black hole in the centre of the galaxy M87. The observations resulting in the final image were carried out at a wavelength $\lambda = 1.3$ mm where the interstellar extinction is not prohibitively large.

parts.question: How large an instrument would be needed to resolve the shadow of a supermassive black hole in the centre of a galaxy? Express the result as a function of the distance $d$ and the mass $M$ of the black hole.
parts.reference:
The scale of the black hole shadow is set by the Schwarzschild radius $R_S = 2GM/c^2$. The light ring radius is $3R_S$.
For a diffraction limited instrument the angular resolution is bounded by
$$\theta_{\text{res}} = \frac{2R}{d} \ge \frac{1.22\lambda}{D}$|
where $\lambda$ is the wavelength and $D$ is the diameter of the instrument.
Using the expression for the Schwarzschild radius:
$$D \ge \frac{1.22\lambda}{6R_S} d = \frac{1.22 c^2 \lambda d}{12GM}$$

parts.question: Give the size of the instrument in units of Earth radius for (i) the supermassive black hole in the centre of M87 ($d_{\text{BH-M87}} = 5.5 \times 10^7$ ly, $M_{\text{BH-M87}} = 6.5 \times 10^9 M_\odot$) and (ii) Sgr A* ($d_{\text{Sgr A*}} = 8.3$ kpc, $M_{\text{Sgr A*}} = 3.6 \times 10^6 M_\odot$).
parts.reference:
For $\lambda = 1.3$ mm, this gives
(a) $D > 7200 \text{ km} \approx 1.1 R_\oplus$
(b) $D > 6400 \text{ km} \approx 1 R_\oplus$

parts.question: What type of technology is needed for the development of such an instrument? Mark the letter of your answer with × on the answer sheet. (A) Gravitational lensing by dark matter (B) Interferometry with an array of radio telescopes (C) Photon deceleration in a dense environment (D) Reducing the effect of incoming wavefront distortions (E) Neutrino focusing with strong electromagnetic fields
parts.reference: (B) Interferometry with array of radio telescopes

tasks.title: Improving a common reflecting telescope
tasks.statement: A student has an average quality Cassegrain telescope, with primary and secondary mirrors having $\varepsilon_1 = 91 \%$ reflectivity aluminium layers. Consider the whole visual band and disregard any wavelength dependence and geometric effects.

parts.question: What will be the change in the limiting magnitude of this telescope by replacing the mirror coatings with "premium" quality $\varepsilon_2 = 98 \%$ reflectivity ones?
parts.reference:
Let us designate the (unknown) original limiting magnitude of this telescope as $m_1$, and refer to the intensity as $I_1$. The new limiting magnitude is $m_2$.
$$I_2 = \frac{\varepsilon_2^2}{\varepsilon_1^2} I_1$$
Now applying the well-known magnitude formula:
$$m_1 - m_2 = -2.5 \log \frac{I_1}{I_2} = -2.5 \log \frac{\varepsilon_2^2}{\varepsilon_1^2}$$
With numerical values: $m_1 - m_2 = -0.16^m \implies m_2 = m_1 + 0.16^m$

parts.question: Assuming the student also uses a star diagonal mirror with reflectivity $\varepsilon_1$ with the original telescope — what will be the improvement if he/she also replaces this piece with an $\varepsilon_3 = 99 \%$ reflectivity ("dielectric" mirror) model, combined with the new $\varepsilon_2$ mirrors?
parts.reference:
The similar way of thinking gives:
$$m_2 = m_1 + 2.5 \log \frac{\varepsilon_2^2 \varepsilon_3}{\varepsilon_1^3}$$
With numerical values: $m_1 - m_2 = -0.25^m \implies m_2 = m_1 + 0.25^m$

parts.question: Is this difference obviously detectable by the human eye? Mark "YES" or "NO" on the answer sheet.
parts.reference: Yes, it is well appreciable by most human eyes. Therefore, especially the deep-sky-object hunters are using higher reflectivity mirrors in their telescopes.

tasks.title: Cosmic Microwave Background Oven
tasks.statement: Since the human body is made mostly of water, it is very efficient at absorbing microwave photons. Assume that an astronaut’s body is a perfect spherical absorber with mass of $m = 60$ kg, and its average density and heat capacity are the same as for pure water, i.e. $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ and $C = 4200 \text{ J kg}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$.

parts.question: What is the approximate rate, in watts, at which an astronaut in intergalactic space would absorb radiative energy from the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB)? $T_{\text{CMB}} = 2.728$ K.
parts.reference:
If the body is spherical, its radius $r$: $V = \frac{m}{\rho} = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \implies r = \left(\frac{3m}{4\pi\rho}\right)^{1/3}$
The area of the body: $A = 4\pi r^2 = (4\pi)^{1/3} \left(\frac{3m}{\rho}\right)^{2/3}$
According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, total radiated energy per unit surface area: $j = \sigma T_{\text{CMB}}^4$
The total absorbed energy per unit time: $P = jA = \sigma T_{\text{CMB}}^4 (4\pi)^{1/3} \left(\frac{3m}{\rho}\right)^{2/3}$
Numerical value: $P \approx 2.3 \times 10^{-6}$ W

parts.question: Approximately how many CMB photons per second would the astronaut absorb?
parts.reference:
The mean energy of CMB photons: $\langle\varepsilon\rangle = 3kT_{\text{CMB}} = 1.1 \times 10^{-22}$ J
The number of CMB photons the body would absorb per second: $n = \frac{P}{\langle\varepsilon\rangle}$
Numerical value: $n = 2.1 \times 10^{16} \text{ s}^{-1}$

parts.question: Ignoring other energy inputs and outputs, how long would it take for the CMB to raise the astronaut’s temperature by $\Delta T = 1$ K?
parts.reference:
Denote the time necessary: $\Delta t = \frac{Cm\Delta T}{P}$
Numerical value: $\Delta t \approx 1.1 \times 10^{11} \text{ s} \approx 1253200 \text{ d} \approx 3430 \text{ yr}$

tasks.title: The height of the chimney of Tiszaújváros power plant
tasks.statement: The European Copernicus Earth-observation programme operates two Sentinel-2 remote sensing satellites on Sun-synchronous polar orbits at about 800 km altitude. The 3rd tallest building in Hungary is the chimney of a power plant near the town Tiszaújváros. Two Sentinel-2 satellite images show shadow lengths $x_1 = 125$ m (June 29) and $x_2 = 780$ m (December 16).

parts.question: On which date do we expect the shadow to be longer? Mark the letter of your answer with × on the answer sheet. (A) on June 29 (B) on December 16
parts.reference: (B) the one on December 16. At a given moment of the day, the Sun elevation is lower in winter on the northern hemisphere.

parts.question: At which time of the day did the Sentinel-2 satellites fly over this area? Mark the letter of your answer with × on the answer sheet. (A) early morning (B) late morning (C) early afternoon (D) late afternoon
parts.reference: (B) late in the morning. The shadows point slightly west of north (approx. 9:45 UTC / 10:45 CET).

parts.question: Based on the given shadow lengths, estimate the height of this chimney. Assume that the satellite images were taken at local noon.
parts.reference:
$\tan \alpha_1 = h/x_1$, $\tan \alpha_2 = h/x_2$. $\alpha_1 - \alpha_2 = 2\varepsilon \approx 45^\circ$. Using $\tan \alpha_1 = \tan(\alpha_2 + 45^\circ) = \frac{1 + \tan \alpha_2}{1 - \tan \alpha_2}$.
Substituting and reducing: $h^2 + h(x_1 - x_2) + x_1 x_2 = 0$.
Roots for $x_1 = 125$ m, $x_2 = 780$ m give $h_1 = 426$ m and $h_2 = 229$ m. Since $426$ m gives an impossible solar elevation in winter, $h = 229$ m (official data is 250 m).

parts.question: What could affect the accuracy of the chimney’s derived height (more than one choice is possible)? Mark the letter of your answer with × on the answer sheet. (A) The oblate spheroid shape of the Earth. (B) Limited resolution of the satellite images and the ill-defined edge of the shadow. (C) The elevation of the base of the tower above sea level. (D) Seasonal variation in the tilt of the Earth’s rotational axis. (E) Taking into account the effect of atmospheric refraction.
parts.reference: (B) and (E)

tasks.title: Effect of sunspots on solar irradiance
tasks.statement: Since 1978, the solar constant has been almost continuously measured by detectors on-board artificial satellites, revealing seasonal, monthly, yearly, and longer timescale variations.

parts.question: Calculate the value of the solar constant at the top of the Earth's atmosphere, when the Earth is 1 au from a perfectly quiet Sun, assuming that Sun emits as a perfect black-body.
parts.reference: $P = A\sigma T^4$, $I = \frac{\sigma 4\pi R^2 T^4}{4π d_\oplus^2} = \sigma \frac{R^2 T^4}{d_\oplus^2} = 1365.9 \text{ W m}^{-2}$

parts.question: Calculate the solar constant of this perfectly quiet Sun in early January and early July, and find their ratio.
parts.reference: $I_{\text{perihelion}} = \frac{I}{(1-e)^2} = 1412.7 \text{ W m}^{-2}$, $I_{\text{aphelion}} = \frac{I}{(1+e)^2} = 1321.4 \text{ W m}^{-2}$. Ratio = 1.0691.

parts.question: Calculate the solar constant again at 1 au in the presence of a near equatorial sunspot with mean temperature $T_{\text{sp}} = 3300$ K and diameter $D_{\text{sp}} = 90000$ km. Calculate the ratio - blank Sun to Sun with sunspot.
Calculate the ratio of solar irradiance for the cases when the sunspot is not visible from the Earth to the case when it is fully visible.
parts.reference: $A^0 = \frac{P_{\text{disk}}^0}{P_{\text{disk}}} = 1 - \left(\frac{R_{\text{sp}}}{R}\right)^2 \left(1 - \left(\frac{T_{\text{sp}}}{T}\right)^4\right) = 0.9963$

tasks.title: Amplitude variation of RR Lyrae stars
tasks.statement: The light variation of an RR Lyrae star is observed at two different wavelengths: $\lambda_1 = 500$ nm and $\lambda_2 = 2000$ nm, probing layer 1 and layer 2. Wien approximation can be used for black-body radiation: $F(\lambda, T) \propto \lambda^{-5} \exp(-C_b / \lambda T)$ where $C_b = hc/k \approx 0.0144$ m K.

parts.question: Assume that the temperature varies between $T_1 = 6000$ K and $T_2 = 7400$ K in each of the layers and ignoring radius variation, what is the ratio of the amplitudes of variation in magnitudes at the two wavelengths?
parts.reference: $A(\lambda) \propto \lambda^{-1}$. Thus $\frac{A(\lambda_1)}{A(\lambda_2)} = \frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = 4$

parts.question: What is the peak to peak amplitude of the light curve at $\lambda_1$? Use the magnitude scale.
parts.reference: $A_{\text{max}}(\lambda_1) = \frac{2.5 \log e \ C_b}{\lambda_1} \left(\frac{1}{T_{\text{min}}} - \frac{1}{T_{\text{max}}}\right) = 1^m$

parts.question: Ignoring temperature variation, what is the contribution of the radius variation to the light-curve amplitude for a given wavelength, if $R_{\text{min}} = 0.9 \langle R \rangle$ and $R_{\text{max}} = 1.05 \langle R \rangle$?
parts.reference: $A(\lambda) = 5 \log \frac{R_{\text{max}}}{R_{\text{min}}} = 5 \log \frac{1.05}{0.9} = 0.33^m$

parts.question: During minimum amplitude of pulsation the temperature variation is reduced to $T_{\text{min}} = 6100$ K and $T_{\text{max}} = 6900$ K. What is the modulation amplitude at the two wavelengths? For maximum amplitude, use values from part a.
parts.reference: At $\lambda_1$, $A_{\text{min}}(\lambda_1) = 0.6^m$. Amplitude changes by $1^m - 0.6^m = 0.4^m$ at $\lambda_1$ and $0.25^m - 0.15^m = 0.1^m$ at $\lambda_2$.

parts.question: Which statement is correct? Mark the letter of your answer with × on the answer sheet. (A) It is easier to observe the Blazhko effect in the infrared band. (B) The temperature variation dominates the visual light curve. (C) If we neglect the radius variation, the amplitude is inversely proportional to the wavelength. (D) Multi-colour observations are not useful in understanding the Blazhko effect.
parts.reference: B and C

tasks.title: Distance of the Lagrangian point L2 of the Earth–Moon system
tasks.statement: The Chinese spacecraft Queqiao was placed into a halo orbit around the outer Lagrangian point $L_2$ of the Earth–Moon system. Calculate the distance ($h$) of this satellite above the surface of the Moon. The Moon’s orbit should be considered as a perfect circle with radius $R = 384400$ km. Neglect perturbations from the Sun and other planets.

parts.question: Calculate the distance $h$ of the satellite above the surface of the Moon.
parts.reference:
Equation of motion for $L_2$: $\frac{M+m+M}{\dots}$ or using $\frac{M+m}{R^3} = \frac{\omega^2}{G}$ and approximation $(1+x)^{-2} \approx 1-2x$.
Resulting in $x^3 = \frac{m}{3M+m} \implies x = 0.15983$.
$r = x R_{\text{Moon}} = 61440$ km.
$h = r - R_{\text{Moon}} = 61440 - 1737 = 59703$ km.

tasks.title: South → East → North
tasks.statement: Consider the Earth as a perfect, rigid, sphere with radius $R = 6378$ km. Find points on the surface from which we can travel first 6378 km South, then 6378 km East, and after that 6378 km North, and return to the original point. Calculate geographic coordinates of turning points and draw paths.

parts.question: Find the trivial solution (point and path).
parts.reference: The North Pole (N) is a trivial solution.

parts.question: Find the coordinates of the turning points for $s = 6378$ km (a-type curve starting from North Pole).
parts.reference: $\lambda_A = 0^\circ$, $\lambda_B = 68.09^\circ$, $\phi_A = \phi_B = 32.704^\circ$

parts.question: Find the non-trivial solutions (starting points and turning points) for $s = 6378$ km.

tasks.title: Distance to a Near-Earth Asteroid
tasks.statement: A Near-Earth Asteroid is observed from Nagykanizsa, Hungary (lat 46°27' N, long 17° E) and Windhoek, Namibia (lat 22°34' S, long 17° E) when it crosses their respective meridians. Nagykanizsa observer sees it 25° south of zenith, Windhoek observer sees it 45° north of zenith at the same instant.

parts.question: Draw a diagram of the geometric configuration.
parts.reference: Geometric figure showing points N, W, O, and asteroid A with zenith angles.

parts.question: What is the distance of this asteroid from the centre of the Earth, expressed in units of Earth-radii and the average Earth-Moon distance?
parts.reference:
$\alpha = 55.5^\circ$, $d = 1.13305 R$.
$D = 65.8 R = 1.1 d_{\text{Moon}}$. The asteroid is at 65.8 Earth-radii from the centre of the Earth.

tasks.title: Distance to the Coma galaxy cluster
tasks.statement: The Coma galaxy cluster (Abell 1656) has an angular diameter of about 100 arcminutes and contains more than 1000 galaxies. Radial velocities of 20 member galaxies are given in a table. $H_0 = 70 \text{ km s}^{-1} \text{ Mpc}^{-1}$.

parts.question: Derive the distance of the cluster from the mean radial velocity of the galaxies listed in the table.
parts.reference: Mean radial velocity $\langle v_r \rangle \approx 6731 \text{ km s}^{-1}$. Distance $D = \frac{\langle v_r \rangle}{H_0} = 96 \text{ Mpc}$.

parts.question: Estimate the physical diameter of the cluster (in Mpc).
parts.reference: Angular diameter $\theta = 100' = 1.67^\circ = 0.0291$ rad. Physical diameter $d = \theta D = 2.80$ Mpc.

parts.question: Use the virial theorem to prove that the cluster mass $M$ can be expressed as $M = \frac{5R\sigma_r^2}{G}$.
parts.reference: Derivation using $\langle K \rangle = \frac{3}{2}m\sigma_r^2$, $\langle U \rangle = -\frac{3}{5}\frac{GMm}{R}$, and $-2\langle K \rangle = \langle U \rangle$.

parts.question: Using the data in the table, estimate the virial mass of the Coma cluster in solar masses.
parts.reference: Velocity dispersion $\sigma_{r,N} \approx 1184 \text{ km s}^{-1}$ (or 1214). Using $R \approx 1.40$ Mpc, $M \approx 2.28 \times 10^{15} M_\odot$ (or $2.40 \times 10^{15} M_\odot$).

parts.question: Total luminosity $L \approx 5 \times 10^{12} L_\odot$. Calculate the mass-luminosity ratio of the cluster in solar mass per solar luminosity units.
parts.reference: $M/L \approx 455 - 480 M_\odot / L_\odot$.

parts.question: Which statements are true? Mark with ×. (A) Mass-Luminosity ratio of Coma is much higher than that of a typical spiral galaxy. (B) Similar. (C) Much less. (D) Coma contains much more dark matter than a typical spiral galaxy. (E) Much less.
parts.reference: (A) and (D)

tasks.title: Photographing a nanosatellite
tasks.statement: The Hungarian nanosatellite MASAT-1 ($10 \times 10$ cm aluminum cubesat, mass 1 kg) was in a circular orbit 900 km above sea level. Baja Astronomical Observatory ($50$ cm RC telescope, f/8.4, $4096 \times 4096$ CCD with $9 \mu$m pixels, detection limit $19.5^m$ for 2 min exposure) attempted to photograph it.

parts.question: Calculate the apparent visual magnitude of this cubesat under ideal observational circumstances at zenith at midnight, ignoring atmospheric effects.
parts.reference: $m_{\text{MASAT}} = 9.72^m$ by comparison with the Full Moon and accounting for distances and albedos.

parts.question: Would it ever be possible to photograph their nanosatellite with the existing equipment (ignoring seeing)? Support with detailed calculations and mark "YES" or "NO".
parts.reference:
Angular speed of satellite $\omega_r \approx 1696.8''/\text{s}$. Relative speed $\Delta\omega \approx 1693.3''/\text{s}$. Pixel scale $S = 0.049 \mu\text{m}^{-1}$, pixel size on sky $0.44''$.
Effective trace magnitude $m_{\text{MASAT,trace}} \approx 23.9^m$, which is far below the $19.5^m$ detection limit.
Answer: NO.

parts.question: What would have been the answer if they had taken into account the blurring effect of the atmosphere (seeing FWHM = 3.5'')? Mark "YES", "NO", or "Close to the limit" and support with a short calculation.
parts.reference:
Seeing expands the $19.5^m$ star over $\approx 50$ pixels, reducing its per-pixel flux. The fast-moving satellite image remains diffraction-limited during its transit across a pixel. With seeing, $m_{\text{MASAT,trace}} \approx 19.6^m$, which is near the detectability limit.
Answer: YES.
